mcqs.q: Mandibular movement is described as projected in which three planes?
mcqs.explain: Each of the three perpendicular planes has its own border movement and functional movement.

mcqs.q: Each plane has a border movement and:
mcqs.explain: The border movement is the anatomic limit; the functional movement is chewing within it.

mcqs.q: Posselt developed the envelope of motion by:
opts: Combining the border movements of all three planes
mcqs.explain: He was first to describe the extremes of mandibular movement and called them border movements.

mcqs.q: Translation is defined as the state in which:
opts: All points within a body have identical motion
The body is turning about an axis
The condyle rotates in the fossa
mcqs.explain: Rotation, by contrast, is turning about an axis.

mcqs.q: Rotation is defined as the state in which:
opts: The body is turning about an axis
mcqs.explain: The two components of mandibular movement are rotation and translation.

mcqs.q: In the sagittal plane, rotation is limited to about how much incisor separation?
mcqs.explain: Beyond about 12 mm the mandible begins to show translation.

mcqs.q: The terminal hinge axis is:
opts: An imaginary horizontal line through the rotational centres of both condyles
The path the condyle takes down the eminence
A vertical axis through the working condyle
The line joining the two incisal edges
mcqs.explain: Pure rotation in the sagittal plane occurs about this axis.

mcqs.q: Which device has traditionally recorded mandibular movement in the horizontal plane?
mcqs.explain: In this plane the mandible can rotate around several vertical axes.

mcqs.q: In a lateral movement observed in the frontal plane, the working condyle:
opts: Rotates around a sagittal axis perpendicular to the plane
mcqs.explain: It is the non-working condyle that moves downwards and medially.

mcqs.q: In a lateral movement, the non-working condyle moves:
mcqs.explain: The working condyle rotates in place while the non-working one travels.

mcqs.q: Which is listed as a factor having a direct influence over mandibular movement?
opts: The shade of the anterior teeth
mcqs.explain: The TMJ, teeth influence, neuromuscular co-ordination, hinge axis, and the attached muscles and ligaments are the listed factors.

mcqs.q: Determinants of mandibular movement are defined as:
opts: Anatomic structures that dictate or limit mandibular movement
The muscles that elevate the mandible only
The articulator settings used in the laboratory
The occlusal schemes available to the clinician
mcqs.explain: They are divided into anterior and posterior controlling factors.

mcqs.q: The ANTERIOR determinant of mandibular movement is the:
mcqs.explain: Overbite, overjet and the palatal surfaces of the maxillary anteriors make up the incisal guidance.

mcqs.q: The POSTERIOR determinant of mandibular movement is the:
opts: Condylar guidance — the slope of the articular eminence
Palatal surfaces of the maxillary anteriors
mcqs.explain: The posterior controlling factor is the joint itself.

mcqs.q: Posterior occlusal relationships are determined more by:
mcqs.explain: It is the nearness of the cusp to the controlling factor that decides which dominates.

mcqs.q: The TMJ provides hinge movement in one plane, making it a:
mcqs.explain: It also glides, which makes it arthrodial; technically it is ginglymoarthrodial.

mcqs.q: Technically, the TMJ is classified as a:
mcqs.explain: It both hinges and glides.

mcqs.q: The articulating surfaces of the condylar processes and fossae are covered with:
mcqs.explain: The articulating surfaces are avascular, like the disk itself.

mcqs.q: The articular disc is avascular and devoid of nerves:
opts: In the area where articulation normally occurs
mcqs.explain: Posteriorly it attaches to loose, highly vascularized and innervated tissue.

mcqs.q: Posteriorly, the articular disc is attached to:
opts: Loose, highly vascularized and innervated connective tissue
The superior head of the lateral pterygoid muscle
The capsule and the synovial membrane alone
The styloid process of the temporal bone
mcqs.explain: That posterior attachment is the retrodiskal tissue.

mcqs.q: Medially and laterally the disc is attached firmly to the:
mcqs.explain: This firm attachment is why the disc follows the condyle in both hinging and translation.

mcqs.q: Anteriorly, the disc fuses with the:
opts: Capsule and the superior lateral pterygoid muscle
mcqs.explain: The superior head of the lateral pterygoid attaches to both disk and condylar neck.

mcqs.q: The two synovial cavities are bordered peripherally by:
opts: The capsule and the synovial membrane
mcqs.explain: They are filled with synovial fluid.

mcqs.q: The disc is able to follow condylar movement during hinging and translation because of:
opts: The loose attachment of the posterior connective tissues
mcqs.explain: The firm lateral attachment carries it while the loose posterior attachment lets it travel.

mcqs.q: In the numbered TMJ section, the biconcave structure shaped to fit both convex surfaces is the:
mcqs.explain: Its biconcave shape fits the convex condyle below and the convex eminentia above.

mcqs.q: The posterior slope of the eminentia is described as having a:
mcqs.explain: Both the eminentia and the condyle are convex, which is why the disk between them is biconcave.

mcqs.q: How many paired ligaments attach the mandible to the base of the skull?
mcqs.explain: The temporomandibular (lateral), sphenomandibular and stylomandibular.

mcqs.q: Ligaments limit the movement of joints because they:
mcqs.explain: They are passive restraints, not active movers.

mcqs.q: The temporomandibular ligament limits the:
opts: Amount of rotation and protects the joint structures
Separation between the condyle and the disc
mcqs.explain: It limits border movements and protects the joint.

mcqs.q: Which ligament also limits protrusive movement of the mandible?
mcqs.explain: The sphenomandibular and stylomandibular both limit condyle-disc separation; the stylomandibular additionally limits protrusion.

mcqs.q: Which is NOT one of the four muscles of mastication?
mcqs.explain: The digastric is a suprahyoid muscle.

mcqs.q: Which three muscles provide elevation and lateral movement of the mandible?
opts: Medial pterygoid, lateral pterygoid and digastric
mcqs.explain: The lateral pterygoid functions horizontally rather than as an elevator.

mcqs.q: The lateral pterygoid muscles function:
mcqs.explain: Each has two bellies with different timings.

mcqs.q: The INFERIOR lateral pterygoid is active during:
mcqs.explain: The superior belly is the one active during closure.

mcqs.q: The SUPERIOR lateral pterygoid is thought to:
opts: Pull the condyle firmly against the disk during closure
mcqs.explain: It attaches to both the disk and the neck of the condyle, maintaining the condyle-disk assembly.

mcqs.q: The suprahyoid muscles have a dual function — they can:
opts: Elevate the hyoid bone or depress the mandible
Open or close the synovial cavity
mcqs.explain: Which action occurs depends on which end is fixed.

mcqs.q: Which muscles initiate the opening movements?
opts: The anterior belly of the digastric
mcqs.explain: The anterior belly of the digastric completes mandibular depression.

mcqs.q: The stylohyoid muscle:
opts: Does not play a significant role in mandibular movement
Is the main depressor of the mandible
mcqs.explain: It may contribute indirectly through fixation of the hyoid bone.

mcqs.q: Bilateral balanced articulation requires:
opts: Maximum teeth in contact in maximum intercuspation and all excursions
Contact on the working side only
Canine contact only in lateral excursion
No posterior contact in any excursion
mcqs.explain: It originated in removable prosthodontics for denture stability.

mcqs.q: In complete denture fabrication, bilateral balance helps because the non-working contact:
opts: Prevents the denture from being dislodged
Eliminates the need for a post-dam
mcqs.explain: Denture stability, not natural tooth function, is the aim.

mcqs.q: Applied to the natural dentition, bilateral balance proved:
opts: Extremely difficult to accomplish, with high failure rates
Simple to achieve with modern articulators
The scheme of choice in fixed prosthodontics
mcqs.explain: Occlusal wear, periodontal breakdown and neuromuscular disturbances were commonly observed.

mcqs.q: The concept of group function evolved when which contacts were eliminated?
opts: Posterior contacts on the mediotrusive side
Canine contacts on the working side
mcqs.explain: Removing the unfavourable non-working loading relieved the neuromuscular disturbances.

mcqs.q: In unilateral balanced occlusion, excursive contact occurs between posterior teeth on the:
mcqs.explain: On the mediotrusive side no contact occurs until centric relation is reached.

mcqs.q: Group function can be advantageous when:
opts: The periodontal support of the canine is compromised
The canine is the strongest tooth present
mcqs.explain: The load is shared among the periodontal support of all posterior teeth on the working side.

mcqs.q: In group function, during lateral movement the teeth in contact on the working side are the:
opts: Buccal cusps of the posterior teeth
Lingual cusps of the posterior teeth
mcqs.explain: Several teeth act as a group to distribute forces.

mcqs.q: Mutually protected occlusion was advocated by:
mcqs.explain: It was based on early work by D'Amico.

mcqs.q: In mutually protected occlusion, centric relation:
opts: Coincides with the maximum intercuspation position
Is determined by the posterior teeth
mcqs.explain: That coincidence is part of the definition of the arrangement.

mcqs.q: In mutually protected occlusion, excursive movement is guided by:
opts: The six maxillary anteriors with the mandibular anteriors
The posterior teeth of the working side
mcqs.explain: No posterior occlusal contact occurs during lateral or protrusive excursions.

mcqs.q: In canine guided occlusion, lateral movement produces:
opts: Disocclusion of all posterior teeth on both sides
Contact of all posterior teeth on the working side
Contact of the non-working posterior teeth
mcqs.explain: The opposing working-side canines contact and carry the posteriors apart.

mcqs.q: In mutually protected occlusion, the posterior teeth come into contact:
opts: Only at the very end of each chewing stroke
mcqs.explain: This minimizes horizontal loading on the teeth.

mcqs.q: In mutually protected occlusion, the posterior teeth act as:
opts: Stops for vertical closure at maximum intercuspation
The only centric holding contacts in excursion
mcqs.explain: The anteriors guide and the posteriors stop — hence mutual protection.

mcqs.q: Posterior cusps in this scheme should be:
opts: Sharp, passing each other closely without contacting
Flat and broad to spread the load
In firm contact during all excursions
mcqs.explain: This maximizes occlusal function without horizontal loading.

mcqs.q: A pathogenic occlusion is defined as an occlusal relationship capable of:
opts: Producing pathologic changes in the stomatognathic system
Guiding excursive movement of the mandible
mcqs.explain: Enough disharmony exists between teeth and TMJs to cause symptoms needing intervention.

mcqs.q: Which is NOT listed among the structures damaged by a pathogenic occlusion?
mcqs.explain: Teeth, periodontium, musculature, TMJ and myofascial pain dysfunction are the listed items.

mcqs.q: Occlusal interferences are undesirable contacts that may:
opts: Produce mandibular deviation during closure to maximum intercuspation
Improve the distribution of occlusal load
Guide the mandible into centric relation
mcqs.explain: They may also hinder smooth passage to and from the intercuspal position.

mcqs.q: How many types of occlusal interference are described?
mcqs.explain: Centric, working, non-working and protrusive.

mcqs.q: A centric interference is a premature contact occurring when the mandible closes with the condyles:
opts: In their optimum position in the glenoid fossae
mcqs.explain: It deflects the mandible posteriorly, anteriorly and/or laterally.

mcqs.q: A working interference becomes an interference when the contact is heavy enough to:
mcqs.explain: It occurs on the same side as the direction the mandible has moved.

mcqs.q: A non-working interference occurs on the side:
opts: Opposite the direction the mandible has moved
Same as the direction the mandible has moved
mcqs.explain: It is described as particularly destructive.

mcqs.q: The destructive potential of the non-working interference is attributed to all EXCEPT:
opts: Improved distribution of load along the tooth axis
Placement of forces outside the long axis of teeth
mcqs.explain: Forces are placed OUTSIDE the long axis, which is precisely the problem.

mcqs.q: A protrusive interference is a premature contact between the:
opts: Mesial of mandibular posteriors and distal of maxillary posteriors
Distal of mandibular posteriors and mesial of maxillary posteriors
Incisal edges of the anterior teeth
mcqs.explain: The oblique force vectors and proximity to the muscles make it destructive.

mcqs.q: Besides being destructive, a protrusive interference also:
opts: Interferes with the patient's ability to incise properly
Stabilizes the condyle in the fossa
mcqs.explain: Posterior contact during protrusion disturbs incising.

saqs.q: In which planes is mandibular movement described, and what are its two basic components?
saqs.a: Mandibular movement is a complex three-dimensional movement projected in three perpendicular planes — SAGITTAL, HORIZONTAL and FRONTAL — each of which has a border movement and a functional movement (chewing). Posselt was the first to describe the extremes of mandibular movement, which he termed border movements, and he combined the border movements of all three planes to develop the envelope of motion. The two basic components are ROTATION (the body turning about an axis) and TRANSLATION (all points within a body having identical motion).

ans.text: Each plane has a border movement and a functional movement (chewing). Posselt combined the border movements of all three planes into the envelope of motion.

head: Component
Definition
rows: the body is turning about an axis
all points within a body have identical motion

saqs.q: Describe mandibular movement in each of the three planes.
saqs.a: SAGITTAL — the mandible is capable of pure rotational and translational movement; rotation is limited to about 12 mm of incisor separation, after which translation begins, and rotation occurs around the terminal hinge axis, an imaginary horizontal line through the rotational centres of the left and right condyles. HORIZONTAL — traditionally recorded with a gothic arch tracer; the mandible can rotate around several vertical axes. FRONTAL — in a lateral movement the working condyle rotates around a sagittal axis perpendicular to this plane, while the non-working condyle moves downwards and medially.

head: Plane
Movement
rows: pure rotation and translation; rotation limited to about 12 mm of incisor separation, then translation begins. Rotation is about the terminal hinge axis — an imaginary horizontal line through the rotational centres of both condyles
recorded with a gothic arch tracer; rotation around several vertical axes
in lateral movement the working condyle rotates about a sagittal axis perpendicular to the plane; the non-working condyle moves downwards and medially

saqs.q: List the factors affecting mandibular movement, and define the determinants.
saqs.a: FACTORS — the temporomandibular joint, teeth influence, neuromuscular co-ordination, the hinge axis, and the muscles and ligaments attached to it. DETERMINANTS are those anatomic structures that dictate or limit mandibular movement: ANTERIOR determinants (anterior controlling factors) are overbite, overjet and the palatal surfaces of the maxillary anteriors, i.e. the incisal guidance; POSTERIOR determinants are the condylar guidance, the slope of the articular eminence. It is the nearness of the cusp to the controlling factor that matters — posterior occlusal relationships are determined more by condylar guidance than by incisal guidance.

head: Determinant
What it is
rows: overbite and overjet and the palatal surfaces of the maxillary anteriors — the incisal guidance
the condylar guidance — the slope of the articular eminence

ans.text: The nearness of the cusp to the controlling factor decides which dominates — posterior occlusal relationships are determined more by condylar guidance than by incisal guidance.

saqs.q: Why is the TMJ called a ginglymoarthrodial joint, and what are its major components?
saqs.a: It is the most complex joint in the body. It provides hinge movement in one plane, which makes it a ginglymoid joint, and it also provides gliding movements, which makes it arthrodial; technically therefore it is a ginglymoarthrodial joint. Its major components are the mandible, the cranial base, and the muscles of mastication with their innervation and vascular supply. An articular disc separates the mandibular fossa and articular tubercle of the temporal bone from the condylar process of the mandible.

list: The muscles of mastication, with their innervation and vascular supply

ans.text: An articular disc separates the mandibular fossa and articular tubercle of the temporal bone from the condylar process of the mandible.

saqs.q: Describe the articular disc — its structure and its attachments.
saqs.a: The articulating surfaces of the condylar processes and fossae are covered with avascular fibrous tissue. The disc consists of dense connective tissue and is avascular and devoid of nerves in the area where articulation normally occurs. Posteriorly it is attached to loose, highly vascularized and innervated connective tissue. Medially and laterally it is attached firmly to the poles of the condylar process. Anteriorly it fuses with the capsule and with the superior lateral pterygoid muscle. Because of the firm attachment to the poles, the disc follows condylar movement during both hinging and translation, which is made possible by the loose attachment of the posterior connective tissues.

ans.text: The articulating surfaces of the condylar processes and fossae are covered with avascular fibrous tissue. The disc is dense connective tissue, avascular and devoid of nerves where articulation normally occurs.

head: Direction
Attachment
rows: loose, highly vascularized and innervated connective tissue
firmly to the poles of the condylar process
fuses with the capsule and the superior lateral pterygoid muscle

ans.text: The firm lateral attachment makes the disc follow the condyle in both hinging and translation, while the loose posterior attachment is what allows it to travel.

saqs.q: Name the three paired ligaments of the mandible and state what each limits.
saqs.a: The temporomandibular (lateral), the sphenomandibular and the stylomandibular. Ligaments cannot be stretched significantly, so they limit the movement of joints. The temporomandibular ligaments limit the amount of rotation of the mandible and protect the structures of the joints, limiting border movements. The sphenomandibular and stylomandibular ligaments limit separation between the condylar process and the disc; the stylomandibular also limits protrusive movement of the mandible.

ans.text: Ligaments cannot be stretched significantly, so they limit the movement of joints.

head: Ligament
What it limits
rows: the amount of rotation, and protects the joint structures — limiting border movements
separation between the condylar process and the disc

saqs.q: Describe the musculature of mandibular movement and the function of each group.
saqs.a: The muscles group into the muscles of mastication — the temporal, masseter, medial pterygoid and lateral pterygoid — and the suprahyoid muscles — the geniohyoid, mylohyoid and digastric. The three paired muscles of mastication (temporal, masseter and medial pterygoid) provide elevation and lateral movement. The lateral pterygoids, each with two bellies, function horizontally during opening and closing: the inferior belly is active during protrusion, depression and lateral movement, and the superior belly during closure, where it is thought to maintain the integrity of the condyle-disk assembly by pulling the condylar process firmly against the disk, since it attaches to both the disk and the neck of the condyle. The suprahyoid group has a dual function — elevating the hyoid bone or depressing the mandible: the geniohyoid and mylohyoid initiate opening and the anterior belly of the digastric completes depression, while the stylohyoid contributes only indirectly through fixation of the hyoid and plays no significant role.

ans.text: The three paired muscles of mastication — temporal, masseter and medial pterygoid — provide elevation and lateral movement. The lateral pterygoids, each with two bellies, function horizontally during opening and closing.

Active during
rows: closure — thought to hold the condyle-disk assembly together by pulling the condyle firmly against the disk, as it attaches to both the disk and the neck of the condyle

The anterior belly of the digastric completes mandibular depression

saqs.a: BILATERAL BALANCED requires a maximum number of teeth in contact in maximum intercuspation and all excursive positions; it came from removable prosthodontics, where the non-working contact prevents the denture being dislodged, but applied to the natural dentition it proved extremely difficult and produced high failure rates — increased occlusal wear, accelerated periodontal breakdown and neuromuscular disturbances. UNILATERAL BALANCED (group function, 20–25%) has excursive contact between all opposing posterior teeth on the laterotrusive (working) side only, with no mediotrusive contact until centric relation, distributing load among the periodontal support of all working-side posterior teeth — useful when the canine's periodontal support is compromised. MUTUALLY PROTECTED (canine guided, 60–70%) has centric relation coinciding with maximum intercuspation, the six maxillary anteriors with the mandibular anteriors guiding excursion, and no posterior contact in any lateral or protrusive excursion.

head: Scheme
Contact pattern
Where used
rows: maximum teeth in contact in maximum intercuspation AND all excursions
excursive contact on the laterotrusive (working) side only; no mediotrusive contact until centric relation
useful when the canine's periodontal support is compromised
anteriors guide excursion; no posterior contact in any lateral or protrusive excursion

ans.text: Bilateral balance applied to the natural dentition gave high failure rates — increased occlusal wear, accelerated periodontal breakdown and neuromuscular disturbances. Relieving those by removing mediotrusive posterior contacts is how group function evolved.

saqs.q: Define pathogenic occlusion and describe the four occlusal interferences.
saqs.a: A PATHOGENIC OCCLUSION is an occlusal relationship capable of producing pathologic changes in the stomatognathic system; sufficient disharmony exists between the teeth and the TMJs to result in symptoms necessitating intervention. It can affect the teeth, periodontium, musculature, temporomandibular joint, and produce myofascial pain dysfunction. INTERFERENCES are undesirable occlusal contacts that may produce mandibular deviation during closure to maximum intercuspation or hinder smooth passage to and from the intercuspal position. CENTRIC — a premature contact when the mandible closes with the condyles in their optimum position, deflecting the mandible posteriorly, anteriorly and/or laterally. WORKING — contact between posterior teeth on the same side as the direction moved; it is an interference if heavy enough to disocclude the anteriors. NON-WORKING — contact on the side opposite the direction moved; particularly destructive, because of changes in mandibular leverage, forces placed outside the long axis of teeth, and disruption of normal muscle function. PROTRUSIVE — a premature contact between the mesial aspects of mandibular posteriors and the distal aspects of maxillary posteriors, destructive and interfering with proper incising.

ans.text: Pathogenic occlusion — an occlusal relationship capable of producing pathologic changes in the stomatognathic system; enough disharmony between the teeth and the TMJs to cause symptoms that necessitate intervention.
